Watershed flow patterns will be disrupted or lost, at least temporarily. Some of the 90 springs on and adjacent to Tracts II and III will be eliminated. Pollution of the air and water will be caused by blasting, earth moving equipment, vehicular traffic, exhaust emissions, oil and fuel spills, and other events which will have effects on the suitability of the environment for wild species. Noise levels will increase, potentially disrupting wildlife behavior. During the mining operation, mine cuts (high-walls) may be dangerous to animals wandering in the area, and may alter migration routes through the area. Reclaimed areas will have different carrying capacities for many species, and some species may not be able to meet their habitat needs.
Although revegetation will begin to restore wildlife habitat values two years after mining, many years will be required for the re-establishment of trees and shrubs to provide habitat diversity required by many species. Because reclaimed areas will be smoother than before mining and because reclaimed soils may not be conducive to the re-establishment of ponderosa pine, value as habitat for mule deer may be reduced permanently, and carrying capacity for many other species may be permanently modified. Some species, such as cliff swallows, may not inhabit reclaimed areas due to the absence of essential habitat types, such as rock ledges. If reclamation does not succeed in the long term, or if post-mining levels of productivity are substantially reduced, long term adverse effects on virtually all species of wildlife in the project area can be expected.
